newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mixed success for communists in local Russian polls.
newsitem.headline: Mixed success for communists in local Russian polls.

text.p: Russia's opposition communists on Monday celebrated the election of a candidate they backed as governor of the Leningrad region but their choice was soundly defeated in another poll in the large Rostov area in the south.
Preliminary results gave Vadim Gustov, head of a communist- backed coalition, 53.37 percent in the election on Sunday in the Leningrad region around Russia's second city, St Peterbsurg.

Ousted centrist governor Alexander Belyakov won 33.89 percent of the votes in the region of 1.2 million people, which voted to keep its Soviet-era name when St Petersburg reverted to its pre-communist one.

In Rostov, which has an electorate of three million, reformist governor Vladimir Chub put down a challenge from communist Leonid Ivanchenko. Unofficial results showed Chub leading with 62 percent of the votes to Ivanchenko's 32 percent.

The results represented a mixed weekend for the communists, who are trying to boost their power base in regional elections this autumn after their defeat in the presidential poll won earlier this year by incumbent Boris Yeltsin.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, runner-up to Yeltsin in July, told reporters he was "fully satisfied" with Gustov's victory.
"People know him in the Leningrad region. He's an experienced, educated man and very moderate," he said.
He put Ivanchenko's defeat down to a low turnout of only 44 percent and alleged voting irregularities reported by communist activists who travelled to Rostov.
St Petersburg itself remains in reformists' hands following Vladimir Yakovlev's victory in a mayoral election last June.
Anatoloy Sobchak, a liberal who was ousted by Yakovlev, put the result in the Leningrad region down to Belyakov's failure to improve conditions in five years as governor.
"Over five years, Alexander Belyakov has made the region the worst in Russia," Sobchak said.
He said Gustov had won the communists' support but his programme was not based on communist tenets.
The polls were part of a series of scheduled elections of the regional leaders who make up the Federation Council, the upper chamber of parliament.

The communists hope to cash in on the hardships suffered under economic reforms to increase their representation in the Council, where nearly half the 178 members still owe their jobs to President Boris Yeltsin.

The opposition already dominates the State Duma lower house. Winning control of the Federation Council would increase parliament's ability to block government legislation and overturn presidential decrees or vetos.

The first major governor's election since Yeltsin was re-elected in June was held in the Saratov region on September 1. Yeltsin's appointee, Dmitry Ayatskov, held on to power in the vote, trouncing communist candidate Anatoly Gordeyev.
The communists levelled the score a week later when their candidate won by a narrow margin in Amur, which borders China.
